title: NEXP circuit lower bounds from uniform obfuscation
formal:
Prove or refute the following implication:
\[\text{a uniform polynomial-time, perfectly correct, uniformly secure IO exists}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}.\]
IO means indistinguishability obfuscation for general Boolean circuits, with the source's security definition specified below. Security is required only against uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithms. On 16 September 2026 the user selected this particular circuit lower bound from the source's broader question. The target keeps perfect correctness and removes the stronger nonuniform-security hypothesis under which the source already proves this conclusion.
why: This implication asks whether cryptographic security against one effective algorithm at a time already forces a language in nondeterministic exponential time to resist every polynomial-size circuit family. It isolates the role of nonuniform adversaries in a known connection between obfuscation and circuit lower bounds.

definitions:
An input circuit is an explicitly encoded finite acyclic Boolean circuit with a listed set of input bits, AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, optional constants, and one output bit. Wires may be reused without restriction and depth is unrestricted. Gate types and wire indices are written in a topologically ordered list; the number of inputs and the output wire are included. Circuit size for the obfuscation definition means the bit length \(s\) of this explicit description. The encoding admits ignored padding, so a circuit can be represented by larger descriptions without changing its function, as in the source's Remark 6. Write \(C_0\equiv C_1\) when they have the same input arity and output the same bit on every input. The algorithm must handle all finite circuits, not merely a selected efficiently generated circuit family.

An obfuscator \(\mathcal O\) is one uniform randomized Turing-machine algorithm. For some fixed polynomial \(p\), on every valid circuit description \(C\) and every choice of its fair random bits it halts within \(p(|C|)\) steps and outputs a valid circuit of length at most \(p(|C|)\) with the same input arity. Its randomness can be taken as a uniformly random string of \(p(|C|)\) bits, with unused bits ignored. There is no oracle, advice or secret setup. No separate security parameter is supplied: input-description size, including padding, plays that role.

Perfect correctness requires
\[\forall C,\qquad \Pr_r[\mathcal O(C;r)\equiv C]=1.\]
Thus every random choice of positive probability preserves the entire function exactly, not just its value at a random input. Merely negligible correctness error would be a different hypothesis.

A function \(\delta:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) is negligible if for every integer \(k\ge1\) there exists \(s_k\) such that \(\delta(s)\le s^{-k}\) for all \(s\ge s_k\). Uniform security is the following quantifier order, matching Definition 4:
there exists a negligible \(\delta\) such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time bit-output algorithm \(D\), there exists \(s_D\) such that for all \(s\ge s_D\) and all equivalent input circuits \(C_0,C_1\) with \(|C_0|=|C_1|=s\),
\[\left|\Pr[D(\mathcal O(C_0;r_0))=1]-\Pr[D(\mathcal O(C_1;r_1))=1]\right|\le\delta(s).\]
Each probability includes fresh independent fair coins for the obfuscator and the distinguisher. The running time of \(D\) is worst-case polynomial in the length of the obfuscated description; its fixed polynomial may depend on \(D\). The only input to \(D\) is that description. In particular, the definition does not give \(D\) the pair \((C_0,C_1)\), auxiliary information or a length-dependent advice string. The source quantifies over all equal-length equivalent pairs, not just pairs that a uniform algorithm generates. These choices retain its particular uniform-security model rather than replacing it with a stronger auxiliary-input game.

NEXP is the class of languages \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decided by a uniform nondeterministic multitape Turing machine in time \(2^{a(n+1)^d}\), for some fixed constants \(a,d\ge1\): every computation path halts within that time, yes-inputs have at least one accepting path, and no-inputs have none. P/poly is the class of languages having a family of exact Boolean circuits \((B_n)_{n\ge0}\) such that \(B_n\) decides membership on all \(n\)-bit inputs and uses at most \(b(n+1)^k\) AND/OR/NOT gates, for some fixed \(b,k\). Inputs, constants and output wires are free; depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The family is nonuniform: no efficient construction algorithm is required. Using description length instead of gate count defines the same polynomial-size class.

The conclusion requires one language \(L\in\mathrm{NEXP}\) with no polynomial-size family: for every \(b>0\), integer \(k\ge1\) and integer \(N\ge1\), some \(n\ge N\) has no circuit with at most \(b(n+1)^k\) gates correct on all \(n\)-bit inputs. It does not assert a fixed exponential lower bound. The premise is the existence of at least one obfuscator with all the stated properties; the task is to establish the implication, not to construct that obfuscator unconditionally.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication with precisely the defined security, correctness and circuit models. A positive answer must derive \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) from only the existence premise, without adding nonuniform security or an independent hardness assumption. It need not separately prove that such an obfuscator exists. A negative answer must prove both that such a uniformly secure perfectly correct obfuscator exists and that \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\); pointing to a failed proof or giving an oracle-relative counterexample does not refute the unrelativized implication. A separation of uniform time classes or a lower bound only for restricted circuit classes is insufficient. All quantifiers and probability guarantees are exact; no numerical tolerance applies.

source_formulation.text: Section 9 asks whether circuit lower bounds follow from obfuscation secure against uniform efficient algorithms. The user selected the particular conclusion NEXP not contained in P/poly, under perfect correctness; the source proves that conclusion under stronger security against nonuniform polynomial-size circuits.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation transforms a circuit into another circuit with the same input-output behavior. For two equivalent source circuits of the same size, efficient distinguishers should not be able to tell which one was transformed. It does not promise to hide facts already revealed by evaluating the function.

Uniform and nonuniform security differ in what an adversary may possess. A uniform adversary is one algorithm for all input lengths. A nonuniform adversary may use a separately selected circuit or advice string at every length. The proposed theorem would turn the former security assumption into a lower bound against the latter computational model.

The source’s Theorem 1, restated and proved as Theorem 28, already implies \(\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) from perfectly correct obfuscation secure against nonuniform circuits. It also gives fixed-degree lower bounds for NP. These are conditional theorems with a stronger security premise, not solutions to the uniform-security question.

Under uniform security, Theorem 3/30 instead gives \(\mathrm{ZPEXP}\ne\mathrm{BPP}\). Here ZPEXP allows zero-error randomized computation with expected exponential time, and BPP allows two-sided error at most \(1/3\) in worst-case polynomial time. That separation concerns uniform algorithms and does not by itself establish the selected nonuniform circuit lower bound.

Williams’s unconditional NEXP lower bound concerns ACC: constant-depth circuits with unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and fixed-modulus counting gates. It is a major restricted-circuit result, while P/poly in this card permits arbitrary polynomial-depth circuits.

The June 2026 implicit-MCSP manuscript combines subexponential obfuscation security against nonuniform adversaries with an additional proof-complexity assumption. Its hypotheses and conclusion differ from the selected implication; it does not remove the uniform/nonuniform gap here.

The original question did not specify the desired circuit lower bound. The user chose the NEXP conclusion on 16 September 2026. This is an explicit specialization, not a claim that every possible answer to the broader source question would meet this criterion.
